title: Astrid and the Postcards
premise: Zephyrine Oyelaran, a translator who has spent thirty years smoothing himself into English, hears an unrecorded song from his childhood playing on a Lagos radio station — a song his mother wrote and never sang for anyone but him. The broadcast pulls him back to the old neighborhood, where the postcards she mailed him during her final illness have been sitting unanswered in a cousin's drawer. As the last bus route to the district is rerouted forever, Zephyrine must translate not just words but the silence between them, confronting the duty that made him leave and the love he abandoned to survive. He ends by recording the song himself — imperfectly, in a language half-forgotten — and mailing a postcard of his own to a niece who still speaks it.
about_author: Petra Okafor is a former radio archivist who grew up between two languages and one city. She writes about the things families say by mail instead of aloud.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. In his London flat, we watch him work: translating a novel's dialogue into flawless, bloodless English while dodging a phone call from Lagos. A colleague's innocent question about his 'first language' earns them the perfected smile. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being fluent in everything except oneself.

chapters.title: A Song With No Author
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Late-night radio while he proofreads; a melody rises out of static that he knows before he knows why — his mother's unfinished song, sung by a stranger. He sits motionless until dawn. Emotional beat: vertigo, the past arriving without permission.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, with flashbacks. He tries to write down the lyrics and finds the vocabulary gone — he reaches for childhood words and retrieves only their English shadows. His sister's voicemail goes unreturned. Emotional beat: grief disguised as forgetfulness.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Kept Everything
chapters.summary: Phone call, mostly Zephyrine's POV with Tunde's voice breaking through. Cousin Tunde reveals their aunt kept a shoebox: forty-one postcards from Zephyrine's mother, all addressed to him, none forwarded. Emotional beat: shame arriving as information.

chapters.title: Forty-One Postcards
chapters.summary: Tunde reads three postcards aloud over the line; Zephyrine transcribes them into his translation notebook like source text. The last one is dated nine days before her death. Emotional beat: the horror of love received on schedule and ignored.

chapters.title: The Last Bus to Surulere
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. News breaks that the old neighborhood's bus route will be rerouted next month — the district is being rezoned. He books a flight he cannot afford, telling no one. Emotional beat: duty finally pointing homeward instead of away.

chapters.title: Arrival, Harmattan Season
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Lagos in dust-hazed December; the city has grown taller and stranger. Tunde meets him at the airport, and their first conversation happens in careful, mutual English. Emotional beat: home as a foreign country.

chapters.title: The Shoebox
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. In Tunde's front room he opens the box: postcards, a cassette labeled in his mother's handwriting, a child's drawing he made at seven and doesn't remember making. Emotional beat: tenderness with teeth.

chapters.title: What the Postcards Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, interwoven with full postcard texts. Reading them in sequence, he reconstructs her decline — and discovers she wrote about him to relatives as if he'd replied. She invented his answers. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: The Woman on the Radio
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Funmi Adeyemi, the singer who recorded the song, remembers hearing it hummed by a dying woman in a hospital corridor twenty years ago and never learning her name. Emotional beat: guilt of the accidental custodian.

chapters.title: Two Translators
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Funmi meet at the radio station. She plays him her rough recording; his mother's voice hums underneath, barely audible. He realizes the song was finished after all — just never for an audience. Emotional beat: awe cracking open grief.

chapters.title: Duty, An Inventory
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Flashback chapter: young Zephyrine choosing the scholarship over staying when his mother first fell ill, his father's voice — go, be someone — ringing in his ears. Emotional beat: understanding, not excusing, his younger self.

chapters.title: The Rerouting
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs: neighbors petition against the bus reroute; Tunde's shop sits in the path of demolition. The deadline sharpens — the neighborhood itself is being translated out of existence. Emotional beat: communal dread.

chapters.title: Language Lessons
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. He begins relearning his mother tongue from a teenage niece, Ayomide, who mocks his accent gently and refuses to let him switch to English. Emotional beat: humiliation as a door back in.

chapters.title: The Cassette
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. He finds a working player; the tape holds his mother singing the whole song once, then stopping mid-verse, saying his name, and going quiet. He listens eleven times. Emotional beat: the wound located precisely.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Tunde argue on the roof at night: Tunde stayed, buried the aunt, kept the box, and resents being the family's archive; Zephyrine left and resents being its ghost. Old wounds spoken plainly at last. Emotional beat: brotherhood through combat.

chapters.title: Ayomide's Question
chapters.summary: Ayomide's POV. She asks why he never answered the postcards, and he tells her the truth for the first time — that answering meant admitting his mother was dying, and he couldn't do both that and become someone. Emotional beat: confession as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Last Route
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Final day of the old bus line; the neighborhood rides it end to end in a loose procession of grief and celebration. Zephyrine sings the song quietly at the back, in Yoruba, badly. Emotional beat: public mourning, private repair.

chapters.title: Recording
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Funmi's POV alternating. In the station studio they record the song properly: her voice, his mother's humming beneath, his spoken translation of the verse she never finished. Emotional beat: making the private thing shareable without losing it.

chapters.title: What Was Written Back
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. He writes forty-two postcards — one reply for each she sent — and mails them to every relative on her list, each containing a verse of the song in her handwriting's memory. Emotional beat: restitution, word by word.

chapters.title: The Verse He Finished
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Alone in his mother's ruined room, he completes the unfinished verse in her language — not perfectly, but truthfully — and speaks it aloud to the empty house. Emotional beat: forgiveness of self, earned not granted.

chapters.title: Postscript, Forwarded
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ayomide's POV months later: a postcard arrives in London-addressed care of Zephyrine, forwarded onward to her — the first of a new correspondence. The song plays on the radio; she recognizes it instantly. Emotional beat: inheritance continuing, language alive.
